posts.body: I think parts only add up to another thing in certain arrangements. A working bicycle counts, but my left shoe plus a distant pebble does not make an extra object.
I think musical composition can produce great work without expressing whatever the composer was feeling. I can enjoy a carefully built melody without treating it like a diary entry.
Looking at my desk, I count the assembled lamp as something over and above its pieces. I do not count every random assortment of stuff as another thing.
The assembly instructions got me thinking about this again. Some pieces really do form a larger object together; other collections are just things we have decided to list together.
I think a belief can be justified partly because the process producing it actually works. I do not need to discover that reliability just by inspecting my own thoughts.
For me, whether a belief is justified comes down entirely to what I can reach by reflecting on my own mental life. Facts outside that access cannot supply the justification.
I trust my vision in ordinary daylight even without an argument about how my eyes work. Their actual dependability can help justify what I believe.
The reliable thermometer example makes sense to me. A belief can have support from how it was formed even when that support is hidden from the believer.
I think there really is a particular moment that is happening now. Being present is a feature of the world itself, beyond where I happen to stand in time.
I see time as nothing beyond events standing before or after other events. There is no extra fact selecting one moment as the objectively present one.
Two people can disagree about what is happening now, but I think there is still a real present. Their disagreement does not erase that feature of reality.
I cannot reduce the present to a label on a calendar. To me, one moment actually has that status, even if describing it scientifically is difficult.
I think whatever actually exists has to be something concrete somewhere in space and time. Numbers are useful ways of talking, not additional things in a separate realm.
I think numbers and sets really exist, even though they have no position or date. Reality includes abstract things beyond everything located in space and time.
When I calculate a total, I am not interacting with a timeless number object. As far as I am concerned, existing things are all concrete.
The idea of a separate place for mathematical entities never works for me. I think our notation does a job without adding anything beyond the concrete world.
I would take both boxes in Newcomb. Whatever the predictor already put inside is settled, and picking up the clear box adds another thousand to that amount.
Could taking only the opaque box be the rational move because of how accurate the predictor is? I am asking how that argument works, not endorsing its conclusion.
I still choose both in that prediction puzzle. Leaving the visible money behind cannot change a deposit that has already happened.
The predictor can be incredibly good and I would still grab the pair. At decision time, I see the extra thousand as available whatever is hidden.
I tried putting leftover rice in the waffle maker today. The cleanup was annoying, but the crispy edges almost made it worth doing again.
My bus arrived early for once, which somehow meant I missed it. I got a decent walk out of the whole thing at least.
I finally beat the boss that kept flattening me all weekend. Turns out I had completely ignored the upgrade menu.
The new season started pretty slowly for me. I still like the apartment setting, so I will probably give it another couple of episodes.
I bought a tiny desk fan and now every loose receipt in my room has migrated behind the monitor.
I keep forgetting how much better toast tastes when I actually wait for the butter to soften. Breakfast required unexpected patience today.
I think philosophy has come a long way. We have much better arguments and distinctions now, and that adds up to a substantial amount of progress.
I am less confident about calling the progress huge after reading those old debates again. The smaller gains account has some appeal, but I have not settled on it.
I keep finding old arguments that newer work improves in major ways. That is enough for me to say philosophy has advanced a great deal.
I count exposing a bad question as a real achievement too. Add those breakthroughs to better theories and I see a lot of philosophical progress.
I think every fact has some explanation, even when we have absolutely no way to find it. An unanswered why does not mean there is no answer.
I still think there is a reason for every fact. Our investigations can run out of steam long before the explanations themselves run out.
When someone calls an event inexplicable, I hear a limit on what we know. I believe there is always something that accounts for it.
I do not need every explanation to be available in a textbook. My view is simply that each fact has one, whether anyone discovers it or not.
I think the continuum hypothesis has a definite truth value. There is a right answer about whether an infinite size falls between the integers and the real numbers.

To me, alternative mathematical universes leave that particular conjecture unsettled in reality itself. Neither verdict is privileged; extra axioms establish a framework rather than uncover a uniquely correct outcome.
I do not take independence from our usual axioms to mean the continuum hypothesis is genuinely undecided. I think it is true or false anyway.
The question about an intermediate infinite size seems perfectly definite to me. Our inability to prove an answer does not remove the answer that exists.
I think natural selection primarily acts on whole organisms. The creature surviving and reproducing is the basic unit, even though its traits have genetic causes.
I think genes are the basic units of natural selection. The survival of an organism matters because it affects which genetic variants get copied onward.
Watching animals compete for food reinforces my view that the organism is the main unit being selected. It is the entire animal that succeeds or fails.
I would build the explanation around organisms and their reproductive success. For me, genes help explain the differences without becoming the primary targets of selection.
I think someone can sincerely believe they ought to do something and feel no motivation whatsoever to do it. Making the judgment does not guarantee any desire.
I can picture a person fully accepting a moral obligation while having zero drive to follow it. To me, sincere judgment alone does not supply motivation.
I see no contradiction in saying I really should help while lacking even the slightest urge to help. Knowing my duty and wanting to act can come apart.
The completely unmoved person seems possible to me. They can genuinely judge an action required without that judgment producing any motivation at all.
I made soup with far too much ginger, then kept adding other ingredients to rescue it. I now have enough soup for several lunches.
I started a farming game for something relaxing and immediately made a spreadsheet for planting schedules. Apparently this is how I unwind.
My headphones survived a trip through the washing machine. The left side sounds strange now, but I expected a much worse outcome.
I switched my usual grocery trip to the evening. The shelves were picked over, but getting through the checkout without a line felt amazing.
I watched three episodes before realizing I had started on season two. That explains why everybody seemed so upset about things I never saw.
I rearranged my room and finally have space to open the closet properly. Moving the desk took longer than all the other furniture combined.
I would take just the opaque box in Newcomb. With a predictor that accurate, taking the single box is the sensible way to go for the million.
I would take both boxes. The hidden money has already been placed or withheld, so collecting the visible thousand is the rational choice either way.
I pick the opaque box alone in that setup. I take the predictor seriously enough that the one-box strategy looks like the rational bet.
I would leave the clear box sitting there. Given the prediction record, choosing only the hidden box is how I would rationally approach it.

I spent Saturday clearing out the cupboard under the stairs, where apparently I have been storing empty delivery boxes like a tiny warehouse. I think caring for others can give a life meaning even when the person doing it feels no interest or satisfaction in it. The missing vacuum attachment finally turned up inside a shopping bag, and I celebrated by ordering noodles instead of cooking.

I got home late because the train stopped between stations, and the person beside me spent most of the delay describing a sandwich shop. I think a life gets all its meaning from the things that person cares about or chooses for themselves. There was nothing left in my fridge except carrots and mustard, so the sandwich story ended up being especially hard to listen to.

I helped sort donated coats this weekend and somehow came home with a pocket full of spare buttons, which are now rattling around in my washing machine. I think some activities, like keeping people warm, add meaning to a life whether or not the person doing them cares about them. My shoes were soaked by the time I got home, so the rest of the afternoon went to drying everything near the radiator.

I found an old library receipt tucked into my jacket while looking for a missing earbud, then got distracted trying to remember why I had borrowed a book about canals. I think doing certain worthwhile things makes your life meaningful independently of your own enthusiasm or preferences. The earbud was under the sofa the whole time, along with enough crumbs to make me finally drag out the vacuum.
I think genes are the fundamental players in natural selection. Organisms are how those inherited variants get carried around and passed to the next generation.
I used to put genes at the center of selection, but I have changed my mind. I now think whole organisms are the primary units that selection acts on.
The gene perspective makes the most sense to me because copied variants persist across generations. I treat them as the basic units being selected.
I would start a selection story by tracking which genes spread. To me, the animals carrying them are part of the explanation rather than the fundamental units.
I think the statue is just the clay under another description. Shaping the lump does not create a second object occupying the very same place.
I think the statue and its clay are two distinct objects in one location. They coincide right now, but they are not identical things.
I would count one thing on the sculptor's table. Calling it a lump or calling it a statue picks out the same object for me.
If the sculptor squashes the figure, I see that as changing one object. The artwork and the material were one thing all along.
I think believing and wanting involve standing in different relations to representations inside our minds. A belief is not fundamentally just a pattern in how we behave.
I still think beliefs and desires relate us to internal representations, but those representations need not be words or sentences. A maplike mental format could do the job too.
I can keep a belief private and never act on it. To me, what makes it a belief is my relation to an internal representation.
I think wanting the window open involves a mental representation of that situation. The desire consists in how I relate to that representation, not just what I might do.
I tried baking bread in the small loaf tin and it rose straight over the sides. It looks ridiculous but makes excellent toast.
I spent most of the evening changing the controls in a racing game. Once I finally started a race, I forgot which button did what.
I took the longer route home because the usual street was being resurfaced. There is a surprisingly good little bakery along the detour.
I washed all my bedding and then realized the dryer was out of order. My room currently looks like a very poorly organized laundry shop.
I am halfway through a detective show and mostly watching for the grumpy receptionist. Every scene at that front desk makes me laugh.
I replaced the battery in my kitchen clock today. I had spent a week checking the wrong time before remembering it had stopped.
I think philosophy has improved a little over the centuries, but the gains are fairly limited. Better terminology and a few cleared-up disputes count as modest progress to me.
I am starting to doubt whether I have been underrating philosophy's achievements. The case for much bigger gains is tempting, though I am still unsure how far it goes.
I see some useful improvements when I compare old debates with current ones. I would still describe the overall progress as modest.
I do not think philosophy has stood completely still. Some arguments are sharper now, but my assessment is that the total advance has been fairly small.
I think disputes about what exists have real answers that the world determines. They go deeper than picking definitions or deciding how we prefer to talk.

I think genuine existence disputes have answers fixed by reality, although people sometimes mistake a vocabulary disagreement for one. I would sort out the wording before tackling the substantive question.
I cannot settle what there is just by opening a dictionary. To me, the structure of the world makes an existence claim right or wrong.
I think an existence debate can uncover something real even when nobody changes their vocabulary. The answer comes from how reality is put together.
I think every substantial thing we know about the world ultimately comes through sensory experience. Reason can organize the information, but it cannot supply that knowledge entirely on its own.
I think reason alone can tell us some substantial things about the world. At least some genuine knowledge does not ultimately depend on anything we sense.
Even a very abstract scientific argument starts somewhere with observation, in my view. All our substantive knowledge of reality ultimately owes something to the senses.
I do not think sitting and reasoning without experiential input can reveal substantial facts about the world. Somewhere in the chain, sensory experience has to enter.
I think there is an explanation for every fact. We might never get access to it, but reality does not contain facts with no reason behind them at all.
I still think every fact can be accounted for by something. A permanent gap in our knowledge would not make the fact itself explanationless.
I cannot infer that something has no explanation just because nobody can explain it. My view is that every fact has an answer to why.
I think even the facts at the edges of our best theories have explanations. Running out of scientific tools does not mean reality runs out of reasons.
I think there are two things on that sculptor's stand: the statue and the clay lump. They share a location, but that does not make them the same object.
Could the statue and the clay simply be one object with two descriptions? I am asking whether that approach handles reshaping, rather than saying I accept it.
I count the clay and the artwork separately even while they occupy exactly the same space. To me, sharing material is not the same as being identical.
I think the lump can survive being flattened while the statue cannot. That difference makes me treat them as distinct objects, despite their current overlap.
I tried a different brand of coffee because it was on sale. It smells great, but I cannot seem to make a cup that tastes right.
I finally organized the cables behind my desk. Everything looks neat until I move the chair and discover one more wire caught around a wheel.
I went for a run before breakfast and got caught in a sudden shower. The dry socks afterward were easily the best part.
I started rewatching a sitcom while folding laundry. I got through four episodes and somehow folded only two shirts and a towel.
I bought frozen dumplings for an easy dinner, then spent ages making a dipping sauce. At least the extra sauce should last a few days.
I downloaded a puzzle game for the train ride and missed my stop by two stations. That final level was much harder than it looked.
I think a painting can be beautiful even if nobody ever sees it. Its artistic quality belongs to the work itself; an empty gallery doesn't somehow switch that quality off.

I've changed my mind about beauty being there all by itself. I now think artistic worth comes from how people experience a work. Without any possible audience response, there's no aesthetic value waiting inside it.
That forgotten mural still has artistic merit, as far as I'm concerned. Getting ignored doesn't remove the quality it already has, any more than getting popular automatically adds quality.
I don't think everyone disliking a sculpture would settle whether it's good art. People can miss something that's actually there in the piece, including its beauty.
I don't buy a final stopping point where something just happens for absolutely no reason. For any fact, I think there's an explanation, even if we'll never manage to find it.

I'm less confident that every fact needs an explanation these days. The idea of something just being the case has more pull than it used to, but I haven't decided that any facts actually lack explanations.
When someone says the initial conditions just were that way, I still want to ask why. I think there's an answer behind those conditions too, whether or not we're equipped to uncover it.
My ignorance about why something happened isn't a feature of the thing itself. I take unexplained facts to be gaps in our understanding, with an explanation there to be found.
I judge an action by how things turn out for everyone affected. The right move is whichever option brings about the best total result, even when that means breaking a familiar rule.

I think doing the right thing starts with our duties and other people's rights. Those are binding even when ignoring them would produce a better overall result; a good payoff doesn't make a violation right.
If telling a lie would genuinely leave everyone better off than telling the truth, I'd call the lie right. For me, the final balance of consequences is what decides it.
I treat moral rules as useful shortcuts for getting good results. When following a rule would give a worse outcome than another available choice, I think we should choose the better outcome.

I think everything we actually know about the world ultimately comes through experience. Reason helps organize the material, but it can't supply substantive knowledge of reality without anything coming in through the senses.

The author I was reading argues that thinking alone can reveal substantial truths about reality, without sensory input. I'm describing her position here, not signing onto it; I still need experience doing the grounding work.
Even when I work something out from my desk, the premises about the world came from observation somewhere along the way. I don't see that as knowledge springing from pure thought.
I can imagine a perfectly tidy argument about how nature works and still need evidence that its starting points are true. My view is that worldly knowledge always traces back to sensory contact.

My kitchen light finally stopped flickering after I replaced the bulb, which feels like a major household achievement this week. I think researchers could keep ethical and political priorities out of their reasoning, but should deliberately include them. Anyway, I spent the rest of the evening making pasta and trying to get a stain out of my favorite sweater before it dried.

I took the long route home because the usual sidewalk was blocked again, and ended up finding a tiny grocery store with excellent peaches. I think ethical and political priorities inevitably enter scientific reasoning, even when researchers try to exclude them. The peaches survived the walk better than the bread did; I really need to stop packing everything in the same bag.

I spent most of Saturday reorganizing the hallway cupboard and found three umbrellas I'd completely forgotten about. My take is that scientific reasoning can leave social and ethical priorities aside, but ought to give them a deliberate role. After lunch I tried hanging a little hook for the umbrellas, discovered the wall was harder than expected, and abandoned the project until I can borrow a drill.

The new cafe has decent coffee, though the chairs are somehow less comfortable than the bus seats outside. I believe scientists have the option of reasoning without moral or political considerations, yet should choose to bring those considerations in. I stayed long enough to finish my sandwich, then went home to deal with the laundry I'd left sitting in the machine all morning.
I finally figured out why my rice kept sticking. Turning the heat down actually helps, apparently. I've been scraping that pot for months.
My bus went past the stop this morning, so I got an unexpected walk before work. At least the weather was decent for once.
I started that detective show and immediately guessed the wrong suspect. I'm three episodes in and still backing my terrible original theory.
Made soup with whatever was left in the fridge. It looks pretty questionable, but I packed a second serving for tomorrow anyway.
I keep losing the same screwdriver halfway through assembling this shelf. It has spent more time under the couch than in my hand.
The bakery near my stop has these little cheese rolls now. I went in for bread and came home with six rolls and no bread.

I think a belief can be justified because the process producing it is dependable, even if I can't inspect that dependability from inside my own head. Reflection doesn't have to expose every relevant factor.
For me, having good grounds can involve a trustworthy mental process that I'm unable to explain or examine. Whether I'm justified isn't settled entirely by what introspection lets me get at.
I trust a normal visual judgment even when I can't give myself an internal demonstration that my vision works reliably. I think that actual reliability can help justify the belief all the same.

Two people could feel equally certain while only one has a dependable way of forming the belief. I think that difference can matter to justification, even when neither person can reflectively spot it.
I see time as events standing in earlier and later relations. Calling this bit now tells you where I'm speaking from; I don't think there's an extra cosmic spotlight picking out one special moment.
I'm wavering on whether earlier and later relations tell the whole story. An objectively special now is starting to seem tempting, but I'm still undecided about whether reality actually has one.
When I look at a calendar, I think my position changes which date I call today. There's no additional fact making that date universally present; the ordering of events does all the work.
I don't think the universe needs a moving present on top of its temporal arrangement. Events occurring before or after each other are enough, with now working like here does for location.

I managed to spill tea over the craft table before we'd even started, so most of the session involved paper towels and moving everyone's supplies. I think the clay figure and the lump it's made from are simply one object described in different ways. We eventually got the table dry, put some music on, and finished a tray of biscuits while waiting for the kettle.

My parcel arrived just as I was leaving, which meant carrying a ridiculous cardboard box on the bus and getting stared at all the way downtown. I think a clay sculpture and its underlying lump are two separate objects occupying exactly the same space. The parcel was only a replacement lampshade, and after all that trouble it turned out to be slightly too wide for the fitting.

I tried fixing the loose handle on the cupboard today and dropped a screw straight into the heating vent. As I see it, shaping a lump into a statue leaves us with one thing under two descriptions. The handle is still loose, the screw is still missing, and I've put a piece of tape over the vent so the next attempt doesn't end the same way.

The pottery room was freezing this morning, and I kept my jacket on until someone finally worked out the heater controls. I count the clay and the statue formed from it as a single object, however we happen to describe it. After class I stopped for noodles, missed my usual bus, and ended up walking home with the leftovers balanced on top of my bag.
I think some things make a life meaningful whether the person values them or not. Caring for someone can matter in that way even if the caregiver feels bored and wishes they were elsewhere.

My friend says meaning comes wholly from whatever a person cares about or decides to pursue. I can explain why that appeals to him, but it isn't my position; I still think some activities matter independently.
Someone could dismiss years of helping others as pointless, and I think those years could still give their life meaning. Their own assessment isn't the only thing that determines whether it mattered.

I don't think a worthwhile discovery loses its contribution to someone's life just because they stop caring about it. At least some sources of meaning hold up independently of the person's preferences.

I think careful reasoning can sometimes tell us substantial things about reality without relying on sensory evidence. Observation is useful, obviously, but I don't believe every bit of worldly knowledge has to start there.
I still think pure thought can get us genuine knowledge about how the world must be. We don't always need something seen, heard, or touched as the ultimate basis for knowing it.
I don't see armchair reasoning as limited to shuffling definitions. I think it can reveal something substantive about reality itself, even when no observation supplies the grounds for the conclusion.
My view is that thinking something through can occasionally reach beyond our concepts and establish a truth about the world. Sensory experience isn't a necessary starting point for every such truth.
I tried growing basil on the windowsill again. This plant has lasted eleven days, which already puts it ahead of my previous attempts.
My headphones only work if the cable sits at a very specific angle. I spent the whole train ride holding my phone like a tiny tray.
I bought the wrong size bedsheet and somehow didn't notice until the third corner. The packaging is already shredded, so that's a fun little problem.
There's a new shortcut in the game I've been playing, but I crash every time I attempt it. Taking the regular route would be faster by now.
I made pancakes for dinner because I forgot to shop. Added frozen berries and ended up pretty pleased with the whole accidental arrangement.
The neighbors moved their piano away from our shared wall. I can still hear it, but now it sounds like background music instead of a personal concert.
I think believing or wanting something is basically having certain tendencies: how I'd act, what I'd think, and how I'd feel in relevant situations. Those patterns are what the attitudes amount to.

Could beliefs and desires instead be connections to little representations inside the mind? I'm asking how that account works, not endorsing it: what would make one internal representation a belief rather than a wish?
When I say I want a day off, I mean a whole pattern of readiness to plan for it, feel relieved about it, and choose it. I take that pattern to constitute the desire.

To me, believing the bridge is unsafe consists in tendencies to avoid it, worry about crossing, and reason accordingly. It's the organized pattern of thinking, feeling, and acting that makes it a belief.
I think arguments about what exists can be about serious features of reality. Getting our words straight isn't enough; the world itself settles whether the disputed things are actually there.

If existence questions really could be settled just by sorting out our concepts and language, I'd expect a lot of these debates to end pretty quickly. That's a hypothetical consequence, not a claim that the premise is true.
I don't think defining a term settles whether the corresponding thing exists. My view is that there's a substantial answer fixed by reality, and the definition alone doesn't deliver it.

When philosophers disagree about which objects there are, I think they can be disagreeing about the world's actual structure. Some of those arguments need discoveries about reality, beyond clarification of vocabulary.
I think the continuum hypothesis has a fixed truth value, even if our usual axioms don't settle it. There's a definite answer about whether an infinite size sits between the integers and reals.
For me, mathematical reality leaves that gap unsettled: neither alternative wins absolutely. Choosing a framework supplies a verdict within it, but doesn't uncover an independently settled yes or no.
Independence from a set of axioms doesn't convince me the continuum hypothesis is genuinely open in reality. I think one answer is correct, whether or not our present tools can establish which.

I take the question of an intermediate infinity to have an answer already. Our inability to prove the continuum hypothesis or its negation from familiar assumptions is a limitation on those assumptions.

The clock above the pool was broken again, so I counted laps until my arms got tired and hoped I hadn't missed the bus. I think there's a real, observer-independent fact about which moment is happening now. I made it to the stop with damp hair and one glove missing, then spent the whole ride trying to remember where I'd put the other one.

I spent the evening putting old photos into folders, which took forever because half the files had useless names and several were duplicates. I think all there is to time is how events stand earlier or later than each other, without an objectively privileged present. I eventually gave up sorting the holiday pictures and made toast, then discovered I'd left the butter out since breakfast.

My oven timer went off while I was on the phone, and by the time I got to the kitchen the edges of dinner were pretty dark. I believe reality singles out a particular moment as present, regardless of anyone's perspective. I scraped off the worst bits, opened a window, and spent the rest of the evening hoping the burnt smell wouldn't get into my coat.

I tried taking the earlier train this morning and found out the station cafe doesn't open until after it leaves. My view is that which moment is now belongs to the world itself, independently of how we describe it. I ate the emergency granola bar from my bag, read a few chapters on the journey, and arrived with enough time to buy a proper breakfast.
I think natural selection primarily sorts whole organisms. It's the animal or plant as a functioning package that survives and reproduces, so that's the main unit I see selection acting on.

I used to put the whole organism at the center, but I've changed my mind. I now think genes are the basic units of natural selection; their differential continuation is what ultimately drives the process.

A trait has to work as part of a living creature facing its environment. That's why I regard the complete organism as the primary target of selection, rather than treating each inherited component separately.
When I picture selection in a drought, I picture entire plants making it or failing and leaving different numbers of offspring. To me, those integrated individuals are the main units being selected.
I keep bringing too many snacks on hikes. We were out for two hours and I had enough crackers for an overnight trip.
The washing machine makes a new clicking sound during the spin cycle. I checked the pockets and found a coin, but the clicking survived.
I replayed the first level to find one missing collectible and accidentally stayed up until two. Still missing it, which makes the whole thing worse.
My homemade pizza came out shaped like a boot. The crust was good though, and the narrow end made a convenient handle.
I got to the pool early and had a whole lane to myself. By the time everyone else arrived I'd already worn myself out.
Bought a cheap desk lamp and now I can actually see the keyboard at night. Should have done that before spending months squinting at it.
I'd take both boxes in Newcomb's problem. The predictor has already put the money in or left it out, so grabbing the visible thousand improves my haul either way. That's the rational move to me.
I've switched sides on Newcomb's problem. I now think taking just the opaque box is the rational choice: with that reliable predictor, the people who choose it alone are the ones walking away rich.
My decision in Newcomb would be to collect both containers. Once I'm standing there, the hidden amount is fixed, and I see no rational reason to leave an extra thousand sitting on the table.
I know the prediction is supposed to be excellent, but I'd still pick both in Newcomb. Whichever amount is already hidden, adding the clear box raises my payout, so that's what I consider rational.
I think my mental states stay inside my brain and body. A notebook can help me remember things, but it's an external aid rather than an actual piece of my mind.
I'd count a routinely consulted phone as literally helping constitute someone's cognition. For me, thinking can genuinely span a person and their equipment, instead of ending at the skin.
Losing my diary would make remembering appointments harder, but I wouldn't say a part of my mind had gone missing. I locate mental states within the person, even when tools are useful.
I can rely heavily on a map without its markings becoming part of a mental state. In my view, the cognition itself remains in my brain and body; the map supports it from outside.

I think some collections of things make a further object and others don't. Parts assembled into a bicycle qualify; a random selection of scattered stuff doesn't automatically add one more thing to the world.

I've changed my mind about composition needing special conditions. I now think any assortment whatsoever forms another object, including wildly scattered bits. Being an odd or useless whole doesn't stop it from existing.

I don't think every arbitrary grouping creates an additional object. Some parts really combine into a whole, but I take composition to occur selectively, rather than whenever we can list some things together.
Calling a pebble and a distant cloud a collection doesn't convince me there's a further object made of them. I think composition happens in some cases, like an integrated chair, and fails in others.
I count the statue and its clay as one thing. Describing it as a lump focuses on the material, while calling it a statue focuses on the shape; that doesn't double the objects there.
I still only count a single object on the sculptor's stand. The material lump just is the sculpture, even though the two descriptions highlight different features of what I'm looking at.
If I buy a clay statue, I don't think I've acquired two overlapping possessions. For me, the lump that was shaped and the artwork sitting there are numerically the same object.
I can talk about what the clay weighs or what the statue depicts without introducing two things. My view is that it's one object doing both jobs in those descriptions.

The dishwasher stopped halfway through its cycle last night, and I spent a while moving wet plates around before finding the instruction booklet. I think every fact has some explanation, even if nobody can discover it. After getting the machine going again, I reheated dinner and watched the second half of a film I'd started days ago, though I barely remembered what had happened in the first half.

I took a bag of old clothes to the donation bin this morning and somehow came back carrying a secondhand lamp from the shop next door. I think some facts have no explanation at all and are simply how reality is. The lamp works, but the shade is crooked, so I spent the afternoon adjusting it before giving up and moving it to the corner of the room.

My upstairs neighbor was moving furniture before breakfast, so I gave up sleeping in and went out for a bagel while the street was still quiet. I believe there's a reason behind every fact, including ones we'll never be able to account for ourselves. The bagel place had changed its menu, and I spent far too long choosing before ordering exactly what I usually get.

I finally cleaned the crumbs out of my keyboard and found a surprising amount of cat hair for someone who doesn't own a cat. As I see it, anything that's the case has an explanation, however far beyond our reach that explanation might be. Once the keys were back on, I tested them by typing a shopping list and realized I'd forgotten to buy most of dinner.
I tried a different route to the supermarket and found a much quieter street. Slightly longer walk, but I didn't have to dodge delivery bikes.
My controller started drifting during the final race. I still finished, but mostly by steering hard enough in the opposite direction to make my thumb ache.
I cooked way too many potatoes again. Tomorrow's lunch is sorted, and probably the lunch after that if I can find another clean container.
The shower finally has decent pressure after the repair. I was late getting ready because I stayed in there enjoying it longer than planned.
I went to return one library book and borrowed four more. My bedside table is getting crowded, but at least the weather forecast looks rainy.
Found my missing scarf inside a pillowcase while folding laundry. I'd already searched every coat pocket twice and blamed the bus at least once.
I can fully believe helping someone is what I should do and still feel absolutely no push to help. Recognizing an obligation and wanting to follow it seem separate to me.
Could someone explain why genuinely accepting an obligation has to create even the tiniest urge to act? Is that connection supposed to be part of what accepting it means?
When I picture someone completely apathetic, I can still picture them correctly judging their own duties. I do not think that judgment needs any accompanying impulse.
I read an argument treating moral understanding like an engine that always turns on. That seems wrong to me; someone can know what they owe others and feel nothing.

I think inherited stretches of DNA are the basic things selection filters over generations. I think believing or wanting something means standing in a particular relation to a representation inside my head. There is an internal content-bearing structure involved, even when nothing outward happens.

When I silently wish the bus would come, I see that as my mind taking an attitude toward an internally represented possibility. That relation is what the wish is.
I can keep believing something while asleep or unable to move. For me, that fits with beliefs being relations to stored mental representations rather than anything currently observable.
I think genuinely deciding that I ought to do something always gives me at least a tiny motive. It can lose badly to laziness, but it is still there.
I would limit that claim to some motivation, however faint. Accepting a duty does not mean I will enjoy it, prioritize it, or actually get off the sofa.
When I really judge an action to be my duty, I think some pull toward it comes with that judgment. Other urges can easily drown it out.
I separate being moved a little from being moved enough. In my view, sincerely recognizing an obligation guarantees the first, even when the second never arrives.
I think reason can get us to some real truths about the world without borrowing them from sensory evidence. Observation is useful, but it is not the only possible foundation.
I do not think a good reason for an action has to come from an existing desire. Sometimes I have reason to keep a promise despite wanting nothing it will bring me.
I find it plausible that thinking an argument through can reveal something substantive about reality by itself. I do not require every discovery to trace back to a sensation.
I resist treating reasoning as merely rearranging information gathered by the senses. On my view, it can independently supply knowledge about how the world actually is.

I start with the animal facing its environment when thinking about selection. The whole creature succeeds or fails reproductively, which makes it the central unit in my account.

I would rather scientists openly weigh the harm of a missed warning. They could reason without that ethical input, but I think choosing to include it makes their work more responsible.
The point for me is what scientists ought to do, not what they are forced to do. Keeping moral considerations outside their reasoning is possible, and I oppose that choice.

I think some groups of things form a bigger object and others do not. A working bicycle counts for me; a wheel here and a pebble across town do not automatically make something together.

I judge whether an action is right by whether it brings about the best overall consequences. For me, duties are useful guides, but the final test is how things turn out for everyone affected.

I think the statue is simply the lump of clay in a particular shape. There is one object there, even if we have different names for it.

If I point at that clay figure, I am pointing at one object that can be described as a lump or as a statue. I do not see two coincident things.
I think my reasons to act ultimately come from desires I already have. A proposed reason has to connect with something I want, even if the connection takes some thinking to uncover.
